title: My family — possessives that have a dual too
goal: Talk about your family and your job — and pick up two things English doesn't have: special possessives for exactly TWO owners, and the word *svoj*, which you must use when the owner is the subject of the sentence.
bekal: using *moj*, *tvoj*, *njegov*, *njen*, *naš*, *njihov* with endings that match the thing owned
recognizing *najin*, *vajin*, *njun* — possessives for exactly two owners
choosing *svoj* when the owner is the subject of the sentence

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Fotografije družine
dialogs.intro: Budi shows Maja photos of his family on his phone. Maja is more interested in the grammar than in the photos.

notes: **Possessives agree with the THING owned, not with the owner.** *Njen mož* means "her husband" — *njen* shows the owner is female, but the ending is empty because *mož* is masculine. If the thing owned is feminine, the ending follows: *njena sestra*. Two pieces of information in one word.

**Njun = belonging to the two of them.** The dual spreads everywhere, including possession. There are three special possessives for two owners: **najin** (ours, the two of us), **vajin** (yours, the two of you), **njun** (theirs, the two of them). English handles all of this by just adding "both" or "the two of".

**Kako ji je ime? — to her, not her.** Compare with unit 1: *Kako **ti** je ime?* (your name), *Kako **mu** je ime?* (his name), *Kako **ji** je ime?* (her name). All three are clitics, so all three sit in second place.

**Svoj is used when the owner is the subject of the sentence.** English doesn't make this distinction and learners often ignore it — yet it changes the meaning. *Ana bere **svojo** knjigo* = Ana is reading her own book. *Ana bere **njeno** knjigo* = Ana is reading another woman's book. English writes both as "Ana is reading her book".

**Fant** means both boy and boyfriend; **punca** means both girl and girlfriend. Only context tells them apart — and Slovenians have been joking about it since middle school. For married couples the words are different: *mož* (husband) and *žena* (wife).

grammars.title: Svojilni zaimki — possessives
body: Ten forms, and three of them are just for two owners. They all behave like adjectives, so their ending follows the thing owned.
after: *Vaš* is also the polite **your** when addressing someone formally: *vaša knjiga* (your book). Just like the verbs, the polite form borrows the plural.

In everyday speech the possessive is often dropped entirely when it's obvious: *Grem k mami* (I'm going to Mom's) — no need for *k moji mami*. Slovenian saves words here, where English would always say "my".

grammars.title: Svoj — belonging to the subject itself
body: When the owner of something is the **subject of the sentence**, Slovenian requires *svoj* rather than *moj*, *tvoj* or *njegov*. The comparison below shows this isn't a matter of style — the meaning really changes.

head: Sentence
Meaning
Who owns it
rows: Ana is reading her own book.
Ana is reading another woman's book.
Peter is calling his own brother.
Peter is calling another man's brother.
Do you have your own key?

after: The rule boils down to one question: **is the owner the same as the subject of the sentence?** If yes, use *svoj*. If not, use the ordinary possessive.

With "I" and "you", using *moj* or *tvoj* is still understood and often heard — *Berem mojo knjigo* causes no confusion. But with he, she and they, the wrong choice really changes the meaning, and that's where *svoj* needs your attention.

blocks.text: A handful of sentences that cover almost every A1 conversation about family — from how many siblings you have to whether you're married.

head: Slovenščina
Say it
English
rows: Do you have any brothers and sisters?

blocks.text: Notice *Nimam bratov* and *Imam fanta*: the first uses the genitive (*rodilnik*) because it's negative, the second uses the animate accusative (*tožilnik*). Two old rules turn up again on one page — and that's how Slovenian rules stick: by repetition in new places.

*Pogrešam* (I miss) is a verb that takes its object directly, with no preposition: *Pogrešam mamo*, *Pogrešam dom*, *Pogrešam indonezijsko hrano*. It's one of the words people living far from home need most.
Almost every job has two forms. The female form usually adds *-ica* or *-ka*, and using the male form for a woman sounds wrong — not polite, not neutral, just wrong.
To say what you do, there's no word for "a": *Sem učitelj*, *Sem študentka*, *Sem zdravnica*. Two words, done — unlike English, which insists on *a*.

*Kaj si po poklicu?* is literally "what are you by profession?" — and it sounds much more natural than a word-for-word "what is your job". It's one of the questions that comes up most when adults introduce themselves in Slovenia, right after name and where you're from.
